title: Ukrainian soldiers are finding deceptive uses for their unjammable fiber-optic drones as ambush tactics spread
description: Ukraine is using fiber-optic drones in to study Russian bunkers and also shape attacks, a soldier said.
fullText:
Ukraine is using fiber-optic drones in deceptive new ways, a soldier said.

They can gather close-up intel on Russian bunkers and help shape attacks.

Drones that wait to strike are becoming a growing battlefield threat.

Ukraine is using fiber-optic drones in increasingly deceptive ways, relying on their resistance to electronic warfare and close-range video feeds to scout Russian positions, study bunkers and dugouts, and create unusual openings for attacks, a soldier said.

These jamming-resistant drones have been on the battlefield for over two years, and they have become an important tool for both sides, allowing troops to surveil and attack without their drones being brought down by electronic warfare.

Dmytro "Liber" Zhluktenko, a former drone operator who is now an analyst in Ukraine's 413th Unmanned Systems Regiment "RAID," told Business Insider that Ukrainian operators are increasingly using fiber-optic drones in atypical ways — such as deception and ambush — to "create tons of chaos."

He said that some operators have their drones play dead or purposefully lie in wait on the battlefield, exploding at just the right time to kill an approaching soldier or expose a protected enemy position rather than simply flying directly into a target and detonating on impact.

He said fiber-optic drones are also helpful for studying Russian bunkers and dugouts because they can capture high-quality video of "all of the entrances, because you get the perfect footage, you could literally figure out what type of cover that they have on their entry to their dugout, and what you should do to open it."

Close-range reconnaissance is one of the drone's best uses, Zhluktenko said. Before hitting Russian dugouts and bunkers, drone operators can gather "very good intel" and "very precise intelligence at very, very close range."

While they can be used to chase and attack, he said, there are limitations that make them less than ideal for those missions. These drones, which are connected to the operator by a thin data cable, are slower than the untethered FPV drones, and the fiber-optic cables can "break quite easily when you just give it a full throttle."

For fiber-optic drones, pilot commands and video feeds are transmitted through a physical cable instead of over radio frequency connections, which can be jammed by electronic warfare. The cable is delicate and can snap if caught on trees or obstacles. Some soldiers carry scissors to cut through any cables they come across.

A US veteran who has fought for Ukraine told Business Insider on the condition of anonymity that there are "very simple ways to bring them down," including by cutting their wires.

"In the wintertime," he said, "the cold will break them half the time." Still, these systems are considered necessary given the prolific electronic warfare threat.

Zhluktenko said the cable was becoming more expensive, which has limited how often the drones are used. He said Ukraine was finding other ways to try to get the same stable connection, including by using masses of signal repeaters to keep radio connections online, but fiber-optic drones remain in play.

The deception and ambush tactics Zhluktenko described are part of a growing trend on both sides of this war.

A British medic working in Ukraine who spoke to Business Insider on the condition of anonymity said that Russia places drones in positions for ambushes.

Russian drones, she said, will "actually sit within the grass or the verges, and a group of soldiers will either go past or drive past, and these things will literally activate and just almost jump out of nowhere and hit. "

"We have this image of drones flying, making a great noise and making a great presence, but that is not the case," she said. "They can be quiet, insidious, and the one minute you'll be, shall I say, walking along a tree line, the next thing, you hear the noise, and then we see an explosion, and it's just so incredibly rapid. And because they're so fast, it's often way beyond your reflexes to actually react."

Another US veteran who fought in Ukraine told Business Insider that Russian soldiers will use "land mine tactics," where they put the drone next to a road and leave it there, waiting for a vehicle or another target to approach.

Ukrainians have called attention to these tactics as well. Serhii "Flash" Beskrestnov, then serving as a drone warfare advisor to Ukraine's defense ministry, said last year that Russia was using fiber-optic drones for "ambush" tactics, including lying in wait for targets along roadways.

"This is one of the tactics involving fiber-optic drones," he said. "It's effective and causes us a lot of problems." Russia is also using solar-powered drones that can lie dormant for this tactic.

"The drones hide on roads and at intersections," Beskrestnov said. "They're often placed on forest trails, waiting for a target. When they spot a vehicle, they take off and strike quickly, leaving little time to react."

title: FIA wrong to lift Russia ban - Ukraine minister
description: The FIA was wrong to lift the ban on Russian competitors because nothing has changed since it was imposed, the Ukrainian Minister for Youth and Sport says.
fullText:
Motorsport's governing body the FIA was wrong to lift the ban on Russian competitors because nothing has changed since it was imposed, the Ukrainian Minister for Youth and Sport says.

Matvii Bidnyi said: "The reasons why Russia was banned from international sports competition have not disappeared. Nothing changes and it became even worse."

Bidnyi said that the central rail station in the Ukrainian capital Kyiv had been bombed by a Russian drone on Wednesday just an hour before he spoke to BBC Sport.

"The air alert was just turning off," Bidnyi said. "Our kids, we all came from the bomb shelter. These attacks continue almost every day.

"Russia continues full-scale aggression against Ukraine. Belarus can continue to provide military support to Russia. Ukrainian people are still being killed every day. And Russian attacks become more and more brutal.

"I don't understand, and Ukrainian people, and I know that all European people don't understand what's happened, why now we must to make this policy softer."

Russian Athletics files new claim against sanctions

Russia could compete at LA 2028 Olympics

The ban on Russian and Belarussian competitors taking part in international motorsport events was imposed in February 2022, after Vladimir Putin ordered the invasion of Ukraine.

It was lifted on 3 August this year in a decision by the FIA's world motorsport council. This followed the International Olympic Association, with which the FIA is affiliated, lifting its own ban.

Bidnyi pointed out that other sports organisations had not followed this route, including World Athletics.

"When any federation lifts the ban and makes steps towards the aggressor, the terrorist state, it's always really, really sad," he said.

"It's a massive disappointment for everyone in Ukraine. And we think it undermines the collective pressure that the international community has been building against the aggressor.

"Unfortunately, there are a lot of international sports organisations trying to lift bans to release pressure from the aggressor. We can observe it in such a federation as judo, weightlifting, and then a lot of others.

"But we have strong partners and strong principle international organisations - for example, biathlon or athletics - who understand the responsibility of the international sports community for international order and justice."

The Russian Athletics Federation has filed a claim with the Court of Arbitration for Sport to challenge the sanctions imposed by World Athletics.

Bidnyi said: "In Russia, elite sport is deeply connected with the military and state propaganda system. It's one of the biggest whitewashing mechanisms. This is why we call it sportswashing."

The Ukraine government says that the war "has had a devastating impact on Ukrainian sport as a whole - since the beginning of Russia's full-scale invasion: 775 Ukrainian athletes and coaches have been killed by Russia", including three competitors in the Ukrainian Automobile Federation.

It says Russia "has made sport facilities their targets to continue killing - more than 925 sports facilities have been destroyed".

The FIA was contacted for comment. Last week, it issued a statement regarding the decision to lift the ban on Russian competitors.

A spokesperson said: "The FIA has updated the requirements for Russian and Belarusian drivers, national teams, competitors and officials following a vote by the world motorsport council. This follows an announcement by the IOC on 7th July and similar updates issued by other international sporting federations.

"The FIA maintains its ban on organising events and competitions in Russia and Belarus. The FIA continues to monitor the situation closely in Ukraine and reserves the right to update its position in the future."

fullText:
MOSCOW, Sept 1 (Reuters) - President Vladimir Putin said on Tuesday that Russia was winning the war in Ukraine and portrayed the Ukrainian leadership as "terrorists" with whom Moscow could not negotiate.

Putin, in his most detailed ‌comments on the war for many weeks, acknowledged that Ukrainian attacks inside Russia had inflicted real damage and said that drones ‌posed a particular challenge.

But he said that Russia was advancing on the battlefield and told reporters: "I have no doubt the enemy will crumble."

He declined to say when that ​would happen.

Rumours that Russia would be forced to order a new military mobilisation were "utter nonsense," he said.

PUTIN SAYS RUSSIAN ADVANCES ARE ACCELERATING

Four and a half years into the war, Russia controls about a fifth of Ukraine. U.S.-mediated peace talks broke off in February after the United States and Israel went to war with Iran.

Opinion polls suggest growing war fatigue in Russia and influential voices are warning about the strain on its economy.

But Putin struck ‌a confident, hawkish tone as he rattled through ⁠a detailed version of developments on the front line, saying Russian advances were accelerating.

Russian troops had captured 270 square km (104 sq miles) of the Donetsk region in eastern Ukraine in August and two large groups of Ukrainian ⁠troops - one comprising 4,500 to 4,800 men, the other up to 2,000 - were surrounded, he said. Reuters could not independently verify those assertions.

Russia continues to advance towards the cities of Sloviansk and Kramatorsk, Putin said, adding that Moscow's forces were preparing to launch massive strikes against energy infrastructure in Ukraine.

Putin said ​that ​Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy's warning to airlines that Ukrainian drones would effectively shut ​down Russian airspace sounded like "state terrorism" and that Moscow ‌would find a way to respond if it happened.

Speaking at a news conference after a summit in Kyrgyzstan, Putin said it was not possible to negotiate with "terrorists".

He also said, however, that Moscow was open to talks aimed at ending, rather than freezing, the war, and restated its willingness to talk to U.S. President Donald Trump's envoys.

"If someone makes, or can make, a tangible contribution to this process, we are all in favour," Putin said.

"The only thing we would want to avoid is the process spinning its wheels pointlessly. However, if someone is capable of bringing ‌something positive to these negotiations - which, as we understand it, are currently somewhat ​frozen - then, generally speaking, we are not opposed."

Putin specifically acknowledged that Ukrainian drone strikes ​had caused damage to Russian oil refineries, although without referring ​to widespread fuel shortages that have resulted from those attacks.

But he said that the level of protection had ‌improved, and "we only have 10% of our refineries left to ​repair".

Putin responded scathingly to an accusation ​by the German government on Tuesday that Russia was to blame for an attempted drone attack at Leipzig airport last month.

He said the government of Chancellor Friedrich Merz was pointing the finger at Moscow to distract from domestic problems and falling approval ratings.

Putin ​accused Germany of planting evidence in order to ‌frame Russia for the drone attack, but he did not say what he was basing that accusation on.

title: Ukraine dissects Russia’s Zircon missile as Moscow leans on harder-to-intercept weapons
description: A Ukrainian official says Russia's growing use of harder-to-intercept missiles marks a dangerous new stage as Patriot interceptor stocks run low.
fullText:
Ukraine's military intelligence published a detailed breakdown of Russia's Zircon missile.

The assessment reveals its components, speed, manufacturers, and foreign-made parts.

Russia has leaned more on hard-to-intercept missiles as Ukraine has gotten better at stopping other threats.

Ukraine's main military intelligence agency published a breakdown of Russia's Zircon missile, a weapon Moscow has increasingly employed in its intensifying strikes.

Russia has been investing heavily in advancing its missile arsenal, upgrading systems and making them harder for air defenses to intercept. That reaction to Ukrainian air-defense wins now represents a major challenge as interceptors run low.

On Monday, Ukraine's GUR, the country's military intelligence agency, shared details on Russia's 3M22 Zircon missile, including its components and production.

It also provided details on the main manufacturer NPO Mashinostroyeniya, a Russian defense company that is part of the Tactical Missiles Corporation, and foreign parts used in the weapon, which included some made by US companies. The disclosure also named more than 70 companies and dozens of people involved in its production.

In its new assessment, the GUR referred to Zircon as a ballistic missile, a departure from Russia's description of it as a hypersonic cruise missile. New details published by Ukraine describe it as a two-stage ballistic missile featuring a solid-fuel booster and a solid-fuel sustainer for flight.

Cruise missiles and ballistic missiles differ in how they fly and reach their targets. Ballistic missiles typically climb on a ballistic trajectory before descending at high speed toward their targets, while cruise missiles are jet-propelled and fly lower within the atmosphere.

Ukraine's assessment challenges Russia's long-standing characterization of the weapon.

The GUR also assessed that the Zircon is slower than claimed, with a maximum speed of Mach 6.8. Russia claims that the missile can reach speeds of Mach 9.

Russia has previously touted the Zircon missile as one of its "invincible" hypersonic weapons. It first used the missile against Ukraine in February 2024. At that time, Ukraine estimated that Russia had around 40 stockpiled.

The arsenal has since grown, though estimates vary, and Russia has increasingly fired these missiles in strikes on Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities, leaning harder on more advanced missiles as Ukraine has demonstrated it can intercept other Russian systems.

"Since we learned to shoot down more than 90% of cruise missiles and drones with gasoline piston engines, Russia has decided to rely on ballistics and jet drones," Yehor Cherniev, the deputy chairman of the Ukrainian parliament's national security, defense, and intelligence committee, told Business Insider.

Russia did not immediately respond to Business Insider's request for comment on Ukrainian assessments of its weapons and motives.

Cherniev said that Ukraine assesses that Russia has reduced production of Kinzhal missiles because of accuracy issues and instead focused on producing Iskander and Zircon missiles. Russian forces have ramped up ballistic missile attacks on Ukraine this year, including debuting a new upgraded variant of its Iskander series, the Iskander-1000, earlier this summer.

These ballistic missiles are more difficult for Ukraine to intercept, and Russia's growing reliance on them comes as Ukraine struggles with shortages of critical air-defense interceptors. Ukraine relies on the US-made MIM-104 Patriot surface-to-air missile system to confront Russia's more difficult missiles, but it has warned that interceptor stocks are running low.

"This is a new and extremely dangerous stage of the war, which requires us to be more effective in the fight against high-speed jet drones, as well as additional assistance from the United States in the form of PAC-3 missiles for Patriot systems," Cherniev said.

title: Billions in US aid to Ukraine under microscope as corruption rocks Zelenskyy’s inner circle

fullText:
Washington is relying on extensive safeguards and dozens of oversight agencies to scrutinize and protect billions of dollars in U.S. aid to Ukraine amid the country's continuing struggle with corruption, a regional security expert said Sunday.

The oversight comes as President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's inner circle faces renewed political pressure from widening investigations, with several senior officials and aides resigning, being dismissed or facing investigations since 2025.

Zelenskyy dismissed Iryna Mudra, a deputy head of the presidential office, on Aug. 19 as anti-corruption investigators pursued a money-laundering case involving another deputy head of the office.

Investigators have not named Mudra as a suspect, The Associated Press reported.

Zelenskyy Says Putin 'Lost The Initiative' As Ukraine's Tech Industry Reshapes The War

"Of course, in all of the former Soviet Union countries, there is significant corruption," former Deputy Assistant Secretary of State Carrie Filipetti, now executive director of the Vandenberg Coalition, told Fox News Digital.

"A lot more work needs to be done. But we know, at least on the U.S. side, as we're providing support for their military, we have a lot of mechanisms," she said before explaining how dozens of agencies are working on oversight of U.S. aid to Ukraine.

The U.S. committed $67.8 billion in defense articles and services to Ukraine from February 2022 through March 2026 through the Presidential Drawdown Authority, the Ukraine Security Assistance Initiative and Foreign Military Financing, congressional reports show.

That support is part of a broader U.S. response to the war.

About $195 billion has been appropriated for Operation Atlantic Resolve, including funds to replenish U.S. weapons stocks, support U.S. military operations in Europe and provide economic, development and humanitarian assistance, according to the Council on Foreign Relations.

As Trump's Nato Gamble Pays Off, Envoy Names Allies He's Still Watching

"Over 24 federal agencies are involved in oversight," Filipetti said. "To make certain that there are no consequences to the U.S. taxpayer, to our equipment in terms of the corruption issue, U.S. contributions are very much protected."

In recent months, however, senior Ukrainian officials have resigned, been dismissed or faced scrutiny by the country's independent anti-corruption bodies, including Nabu.

Those developments include Andriy Yermak's Nov. 28, 2025, resignation after investigators searched his premises and Mudra's Aug. 19 dismissal during a money-laundering probe.

Former Deputy Prime Minister Olha Stefanishyna was dismissed by Zelenskyy as Ukraine's ambassador to the U.S. on Aug. 3, two days before a suspicion notice was served against her, according to the Kyiv Post.

He also fired Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov on July 15 in a broader reshuffle over internal wartime disagreements which sparked protests across the nation.

Zelenskyy Pressures Us And Europe For More 'Air Defense' Assistance Amid Ongoing War With Russia

In interviews after he left government, Fedorov also complained about what he described as ingrained corruption and patronage networks, Reuters reported.

"We've seen that Zelenskyy is taking really seriously the criticisms of corruption, and every time there is an allegation, he moves very swiftly to remove those individuals from the government," Filipetti said.

"And the fact that there are these independent bodies is, I think, really important. They're listening to them. They're making sure that they're trying to root it out as much as humanly possible."

The Two Most Important American Weapons Systems Nato Is Eager To Have

Zelenskyy has pushed back on suggestions that the investigations implicate him personally.

"The heads of anti-corruption agencies have zero questions for me," Zelenskyy said in remarks published Aug. 23 regarding the investigations. "They understand perfectly well that I am not involved in anything like that."

A February 2024 USAID inspector general review also found that the agency did not independently verify some Ukrainian health workers' salary claims before reimbursement, though Filipetti said U.S. economic aid is now reimbursed only after verification.

"A lot of what the United States has been providing, we're making sure that everything is through a reimbursement mechanism," Filipetti said.

Top Ukrainian Officials In Zelenskyy Government Submit Resignations Amid $100 Million Corruption Scandal

She said U.S. aid has not been tied to the money-laundering allegations and remains protected as Ukraine works to combat corruption.

The scrutiny also comes as Kyiv faces shortages of Patriot interceptors amid intensified Russian strikes and a need for air defense interceptors.

Zelenskyy said he wants to secure 300 additional interceptors for the coming winter, while Ukraine's air force has requested 360.

"One of the most urgent needs that the Ukrainians have right now is interceptor missiles," Filipetti said. "This is why this idea of sending Patriot capabilities and allowing them to produce them on the ground in Ukraine has become so important to Zelenskyy."

Russia's Gas Gamble Backfires As Trump's Energy Vision Reshapes Europe

President Donald Trump has expressed reluctance to further deplete U.S. missile inventories, saying the United States also needs the weapons, while pressing European allies to shoulder more of Ukraine's defense burden.

"We want missiles too," Trump said Aug. 6 when asked about Zelenskyy's requests for long-range missiles and Patriot systems. "Biden gave him so much, Biden gave $300 billion worth of ammunition."

Filipetti also said Ukraine's anti-corruption efforts remain an important consideration for its NATO aspirations.

"I think every country has been really adamant that the Ukrainians move forward in their anti-corruption mechanisms," Filipetti said.

"Obviously, if Ukraine ever wants to be a formal member of NATO, that's something that they will need to prove and demonstrate."

title: Ukraine says its strikes on oil refineries have forced Russia to start importing jet fuel for its warplanes
description: Ukraine has been conducting a long-range strike campaign, hitting Russia's oil and gas facilities to try to hurt its economy and war effort.
fullText:
Ukraine said that its strikes on Russian oil facilities have pushed Moscow to import jet fuel.

Russia has a "shortage of domestic resources" as it tries to increase attacks and fly civilian jets.

Ukraine is attacking oil and gas facilities across Russia to try to hamper its fighting ability.

Ukraine said over the weekend that its strikes on Russian oil facilities have reduced production so much that Russia is now having to import fuel for its warplanes.

On Saturday, Ukraine's GUR, the country's military intelligence agency, said that "systematic and precise strikes by Ukraine's Defense Forces against Russia's oil-refining network have led to a significant reduction in jet fuel production in the Russian Federation."

It said that Russia's increasing air attacks against Ukraine, "combined with the need to sustain civilian air transport, have resulted in a shortage of domestic resources."

"To meet the needs of military and civilian aviation, Russia, which for decades has positioned itself as an energy superpower, has officially introduced a temporary ban on the export of its own aviation fuel and is being forced to seek ways to import foreign Jet A-1 aviation fuel," the GUR said.

That fuel is compatible with a range of Russian military aircraft used to launch missiles and bombs, as well as jet-powered drones. The GUR added that Russia is now fueling its Il-76MD-90A military transport with fuel outside manufacturer recommendations.

The GUR said that Russia had purchased at least 70,000 tonnes of aviation fuel from South Korea and Egypt that was delivered on three shadow fleet tankers. The fleet is a network of vessels that Russia uses to circumvent Western sanctions through hidden ownership, among other methods.

The GUR Saturday said that Russian efforts to "circumvent sanctions will inevitably receive an appropriate response."

Ukraine is conducting a major long-range strike campaign targeting oil and gas facilities inside Russia in a bid to damage the country's economy, which depends heavily on the energy sector, and frustrate its ability to continue its invasion of Ukraine. The strikes have hit targets hundreds of miles into Russia.

Ukraine refers to these strikes against Russia's economy as "long-range sanctions." Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy promised this month that "there will be more Ukrainian deep strikes, which should demonstrate to Russia and the Russians that peace is necessary."

Ukraine has significantly increased the pace of these strikes this year and claimed a host of wins against targets this month, including strikes on refineries, processing facilities, and terminals. The country has said that some sites have halted operations as a result.

Zelenskyy said in June that nearly 40% of Russia's primary oil refining capacity was offline as of the previous month. And he said this month that it remains a priority for Ukraine.

Russia's economy is heavily dependent on oil and gas. Western sanctions have affected the industry, but Russia also received a reprieve when the war in Iran limited other energy sources by closing the Strait of Hormuz, a route Russia does not rely on. Kyiv is trying to restore some of that pressure.

Ukraine has primarily used homemade cruise missiles and drones to hit targets inside Russia. Though Western partners provided long-range weapons, restrictions on their use inside Russia forced Ukraine's booming defense industry to develop domestic solutions.

Ukraine has unveiled new weaponry with longer ranges in recent months to deepen its campaign, including drones with ranges exceeding 1,800 miles.

Mykhailo Fedorov, Ukraine's former defense minister, said this month that Ukraine could be capable of hitting Russian territory with domestically made ballistic missiles within the next three to six months. These weapons typically have longer ranges and move much faster than cruise missiles.

Ukraine is fighting against barrages of Russian strikes on its territory that are stretching its air defenses thin. A key target Kyiv seeks to pursue is the missile launchers inside Russia.

Russia has been intensifying its strikes on Ukraine. Zelenskyy said on Sunday that in the last week, Russia launched almost 2,000 attack drones, more than 1,600 glide bombs, and 31 missiles, including North Korean ballistic missiles, at Ukraine.

Ukraine's long-range strike campaign, which is focused solely on legitimate military targets rather than cities and civilian infrastructure like Russian strikes, has yet to push Moscow toward negotiations for ending hostilities, but Kyiv hopes that the fuel shortages will raise the cost of the war and constrain some attacks.

Russia is slowly grinding through the Donbas as Ukraine braces for a brutal fight over its last strongholds
description: Russia is grinding deeper into the Donbas, where Ukrainian troops are preparing for a costly fight over the region's last major defensive bastions.
fullText:
Russia is advancing slowly through the Donbas as Ukraine prepares to defend its last major strongholds.

Ukrainian commanders say the fight for Kramatorsk and Sloviansk could become brutal battles of attrition.

Analysts warn the outcome may hinge on Ukraine's ability to keep troops supplied under relentless drone and air attacks.

There is a moment before the camera begins rolling when the young Ukrainian commander says, "History is repeating itself for us in the Donbas. Unfortunately." Then he falls silent.

A few minutes later, the man, known by the call sign "Fleshka," takes a seat on a weight bench in the garden of a house in an eastern Ukrainian village, just a 30-minute drive from the nearest Russian troops. Every morning, he benches 80 kilograms here before returning to the screens where he coordinates the destruction of Russian assault units through the live feeds from his drone operators.

"I hope it will be a long fight. This is our land, and we will fight for every meter of it," Fleshka says once the camera is rolling. A few meters away stands his comrade "Sascha," another unit commander with the 33rd Brigade. "It's going to be a brutal meat grinder," he predicts, describing a bloody war of attrition. "But I'm glad to be part of it."

Fleshka, 24, and Sascha, 26, belong to a new generation of young Ukrainian commanders helping lead the defense of the last Ukrainian-held bastions in the Donbas. Both have spent years fighting on the front lines. They were involved in the drawn-out Battle of Bakhmut in 2023 and later took part in Ukraine's offensive in Russia's Kursk region at the end of 2024. Today, each man is responsible for more than 80 soldiers serving in a combined drone-and-infantry unit.

The Donbas is comprised of the Luhansk and Donetsk regions. Russia has captured almost all of Luhansk, while Ukraine controls just under one-fifth of the Donetsk region, an area of roughly 5,000 square kilometers, about five times the size of Berlin.

The question is increasingly not whether Putin's army will seize the remaining Ukrainian-held territory in Donbas, but when.

According to information obtained by WELT from conversations with representatives of a leading European intelligence service, Russian forces could reach the outskirts of Kramatorsk and Sloviansk by early 2027. The two cities form the center of the last major Ukrainian defensive belt in the Donbas.

Intelligence officials predict that Russian troops could complete the conquest of most of the region by next year. The human cost of that campaign, however, would likely be staggering. Hundreds of thousands more Russian soldiers could be killed or seriously wounded in the process.

Since the start of the war in 2022, Russia's military has suffered around 1.4 million casualties, according to estimates by analysts at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, including up to 450,000 dead and nearly one million wounded.

Military analyst Franz-Stefan Gady, author of Attack: When War Comes to Us, offers a somewhat more optimistic assessment for Ukraine. Russia's advance, he argues, is progressing at its slowest pace since winter. "At the current rate, Donetsk region would not be fully captured until the early 2030s," he says.

A slowdown, however, should not be mistaken for a stabilization of the front lines. In some sectors, Kyiv's military position is deteriorating. Russia enjoys local superiority in first-person-view drones on certain stretches of the front, in some cases by a ratio of 10 to one. Meanwhile, 3,000-kilogram guided glide bombs continue to inflict heavy losses on Ukrainian forces in front-line areas.

Gady believes it's possible that Russian troops could reach Kramatorsk and Sloviansk as early as spring or summer 2027, but only under one condition.

"Russia needs mobilization if it wants to sustain or increase the current pace," he says. "Moscow is unlikely to do this before the elections, and if it does, Ukraine has no equivalent response available."

According to Gady, Russia's General Staff estimates that newly mobilized troops need around four months before they can have a meaningful impact at the front. A mobilization this autumn could therefore begin to shape events during the first half of 2027.

Col. Markus Reisner of the Austrian Armed Forces says Russia's summer offensive has so far fallen well short of Kremlin expectations. Nevertheless, Putin's troops continue to advance "slowly but steadily".

The decisive factor in the battle for the Donbas, he argues, will be Ukrainian logistics.

"The single most important capability influencing the fight for the Ukrainian defensive belt around Kramatorsk and Sloviansk is the ability to supply the defenders in those cities. If Russian forces succeed in disrupting those supply routes, Ukrainian defenders will be able to hold out only for a limited period."

Already, much of the resupply effort relies on heavy multicopter drones and uncrewed ground vehicles. Russian forces are systematically targeting these systems while simultaneously attempting to prevent the reinforcement and rotation of Ukrainian troops.

Reisner's warning is stark: "If the Ukrainians fail to break this vicious cycle, the defensive belt will fall." Ukrainian brigade commanders also acknowledge that Russia ultimately possesses the resources required to conquer the Donbas.

"Of course, Russia has the potential," Vadym Krykun, commander of the Lubart Brigade, told WELT earlier this year. "It remains the second-largest army in the world. The question is how far Russia is willing to go, how much further it is prepared to mobilize its economy and its population."

Krykun has been fighting in Donbas for more than a decade. Russian troops first entered the region in 2014, and fighting has continued ever since.

As recently as last year, there were hopes that a settlement over eastern Ukraine might pave the way for a ceasefire or even peace. At the end of 2025, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy proposed withdrawing Ukrainian troops from parts of the Donbas as part of a peace initiative, on the condition that Russia also withdraw and that the area be converted into an internationally monitored demilitarized zone, or "free economic zone." The Kremlin rejected the proposal, which was also supported by the United States.

The troops led by Fleshka and Sascha operate heavy "Vampire" and "Nemesis" bomber drones in the Donbas that can strike targets up to 50 kilometers away. They are complemented by reconnaissance drones, drone-based mine-laying systems, and ground robots.

"Our primary focus right now is eliminating their drone operators," Sascha says. "We located the enemy, bombed the position, and mined the area around it. So I would advise them to leave their foxholes and get as far away as possible."

His soldiers, he says, are doing everything they can to keep Ukrainian infantry alive. "The longer the infantry survives, the longer the cities hold."

Fleshka explains that the so-called "death zone," the area in which soldiers must expect drone attacks at any moment, has expanded dramatically in recent months.

The kill zone now stretches 20 kilometers deep in some places, and up to 50 kilometers in others.

"When they use small groups and start moving, and we detect them, nobody wants to let them get away," Sascha says. "Our priority is to eliminate them. There are so many Russians that they simply do not care. I don't know, it's a complicated subject. We eliminate them without much difficulty, but there are just so many of them."

Sascha then describes the Russian tactic in greater detail.

"The enemy sends people forward one at a time. Ten groups essentially means ten individuals."

If one reaches the designated position, another ten groups are sent forward. Eventually, one gets through, then another, then another, until six soldiers have assembled and can continue advancing together.

"Well, let's put it this way: it's a good tactic. An interesting tactic. I haven't come across anything quite like it before," he says.

According to Gady, this method of gradual infiltration and attrition is central to Russia's approach. "Cities do not fall through breakthroughs or house-to-house combat. They fall through exhaustion."

Fleshka fears that Druzhkivka could be the next city to come under serious threat.

"They have shifted their focus toward Sloviansk. They are already fighting in Mykolaivka."

Sascha also expects a fierce battle for Sloviansk. He insists that his men are ready. "It will be like Chasiv Yar. But how long did they assault Chasiv Yar? About a year, if I remember correctly."

He points to the terrain surrounding Kramatorsk and Sloviansk. "The landscape here works in our favor and against theirs. We hold the high ground and have cover. It will be a brutal meat grinder."

Experts doubt that a complete Russian conquest of the Donbas would necessarily persuade the Kremlin to enter serious ceasefire negotiations. "Putin will adjust his war aims depending on the condition of Ukraine's defenders," says Reisner.

Russia is presently targeting what he describes as one of Ukraine's Achilles heels: the critical shortage of air-defense ammunition, particularly for Patriot systems.

"The first major attacks indicate that Putin plans to subject Ukraine to sustained large-scale strikes this winter. He is following a strategy of exhaustion inspired by Svechin, the well-known Soviet military theorist."

Gady argues that, from Moscow's perspective, the Donbas may represent only an intermediate objective.

"The Donbas is an interim goal, not the final one. Russia's strategic objective remains bringing Ukraine back into its sphere of influence. According to Ukrainian intelligence, planning already exists for future operations toward Mykolaiv, Kherson, and Odesa, even if no timelines have been defined."

A genuine de-escalation, he adds, is politically difficult for Moscow.

"It would require scaling back Russia's war economy and explaining to the population why the war is being brought to an end."

title: A Ukrainian air-defense sergeant says missiles aren't his most challenging shortage. It's the gear that finds enemy targets.
description: Ukraine uses MANPADS to down Russian drones, jets, and aircraft, but to be effective, teams need batteries and ways to find targets.
fullText:
A Ukrainian sergeant said supporting gear is harder to get for his air defense unit than missiles.

It uses MANPADS that down Russian jets and aircraft, but needs batteries and ways to find targets.

Equipment like drone detectors and electronic warfare systems is "hard to get," he said.

The hardest shortage facing one Ukrainian shoulder-fired air-defense unit isn't necessarily missiles, its battery sergeant told Business Insider. It's some of the equipment that helps crews find targets and keep their systems running.

The soldier, who uses the call sign Yankee, serves in a front-line unit equipped with man-portable air-defense systems, or MANPADS, which fire shoulder-launched missiles able to engage low-flying aircraft, as well as cruise missiles and drones.

Weapons like these, which include the US Stinger, Polish Piorun, and Soviet-designed Igla, have been a key part of Ukraine's short-range air defense in front-line areas, protecting troops and operations from attacks.

Yankee said that for him, at least, one of the hardest things "is finding resources. Secondary resources, not the weaponry, but electronic warfare stuff."

He said some of the devices that help his team detect threats and keep its equipment working are "hard to get." What is hardest to find is "mostly electronics."

"I'm talking more about devices that locate the drones and warn you," Yankee said. "I'm talking about stuff like EcoFlows, batteries, big batteries, because we have a shortage of them, just in general, just a mass shortage."

Ukrainian soldiers are increasingly using drone detectors, including small handheld or vehicle-mounted models, to warn of certain incoming enemy drones by detecting their radio frequencies.

EcoFlows are portable power stations that can power or recharge essential gear such as radios and communications equipment, Starlink terminals, laptops and tablets, drone equipment, electronic warfare systems, and sensors.

These, and batteries in general, are especially important because soldiers are often far from power outlets, and Russian attacks often shut down energy infrastructure. Running a portable generator would be much louder and might reveal their positions.

Electronic warfare systems are also vital for Ukraine as it tries to disrupt Russia's communications and jam its drones.

Despite their importance, this equipment isn't always easy for units to obtain in sufficient quantities. Some of the gear is much newer and less readily available than supplies like ammunition. And while demand is high, some equipment still isn't being produced in large quantities. In some cases, there are also distribution bottlenecks that affect availability.

Unlike many Western militaries, Ukraine's military doesn't have a highly centralized system for weapons procurement. Units often buy or receive gear themselves, including through crowdfunding.

There are advantages to this setup for rapid innovation because units engage manufacturers directly, but the system can also result in uneven distribution, leaving some units facing shortages.

Ukrainian foundations, units, and other groups that are involved in sourcing and crowdfunding equipment for troops often ask for gear like batteries and detectors, with some describing them as items that air defenders regularly need.

MANPADS and the units that operate them are important for Ukraine. Units, service members, and officials have reported missiles taking down Russian drones, helicopters, and aircraft, and Western analysts have credited MANPADS with making penetrating low-altitude Russian fixed-wing and helicopter sorties too costly for Russia to continue.

A report last year from the Center for Strategic and International Studies, a US think tank, said that Ukraine's integration of MANPADS operators into its air defense teams forced Russian pilots to choose between flying high and being targeted by ground-based air defenses or flying low and facing MANPAD missiles. These short-range defenses relieved the pressure on Ukraine's ground-based systems, allowing them to "survive and eventually recover."

Yankee's unit provides air defense for infantry who need to get to the zero line, the far edge of the front line, and, as a result, "we participate in battle," he said.

He said that conditions there can be so dangerous that moving just 300 meters can take 7 days of waiting for safe conditions and protection. Moving even that short distance, he said, "can be like a question of life and death."

Yankee spoke with Business Insider at Operation Legio, a Norway-led multinational program that trains and equips Ukrainian forces, including at a purpose-built camp in Poland. He said he was learning NATO standards and tactics, combining Western practices with his existing battle-won skills before returning to Ukraine.

Yankee said he uses the Stinger and Igla systems. Ukrainian soldiers have, at times since Russia's full-scale invasion began in February 2022, reported shortages of MANPADS missiles, saying those shortages allowed Russian forces to be bolder because they knew the Ukrainians couldn't try to stop as many of their attacks.

But Ukraine's military has not suffered critical shortages of them the way it has with larger, surface-to-air missiles, and allies have announced new deliveries throughout the war.

Not everything is consistent across the force though. Ukraine's military disseminates weapons and ammunition according to operational need, so one unit could be well supplied for critical missions while another comes up short.

KYIV, Ukraine (AP) — Russia bombarded cities across Ukraine with missiles and drones in an overnight onslaught that ran into the daylight hours of Thursday, when explosions echoed around Kyiv through the morning.

Ukraine is desperately short of U.S.-made Patriot air defense missiles that can counter Russia's ballistic missiles, and Moscow's fast-flying jet-powered drones have brought another challenge since the Russian military's full-scale invasion began 4½ years ago.

Ukrainian officials say Russia builds up missile stocks and launches major attacks every few days, hoping to exhaust Ukrainian defenses through the sheer weight of numbers. In response, Ukraine has hit high-profile targets on Russian soil as the countries inflict mutual destruction.

The Russian Defense Ministry said its forces carried out a "massive" strike on targets in nine Ukrainian cities that began after nightfall on Wednesday. It described the targets as military-related, including industrial facilities, oil refineries, logistics hubs and port infrastructure.

Civilian areas, including apartment buildings, suffered damage. The barrage killed a 78-year-old woman in the southern Zaporizhzhia region and another person in the northern Kharkiv region, with at least 14 people reported wounded elsewhere, Ukrainian officials said.

"Russia continues to invest in missiles and in expanding its war, and that means more countermeasures are needed," Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on social media, noting promises earlier this week by European countries to provide more air defense assistance.

"It is important that these (measures) are also supplemented by additional ballistic missile defense packages" through European purchases of weapons from the United States, he said.

Though the Russian Defense Ministry insisted only war-related targets were attacked, Russia appears determined to hurt Ukrainian businesses and dent the country's economy through attacks on private enterprise after Ukraine's long-range drone strikes caused financial difficulties for Moscow.

Russian drones hit three major distribution centers, destroying depots belonging to a toy store chain and a confectionery company, and damaging another run by an electronics retailer, the companies said.

In addition, Moscow continued its efforts to wreck the Ukrainian power grid before the freezing winter months.

Four powerful glide bombs destroyed generating equipment at the southern Kherson region's combined heat and power plant, forcing it to shut down, its operator Naftogaz said.

Zelenskyy was due to visit neighboring Moldova on Thursday to mark its national day commemorating its 1991 declaration of independence from the Soviet Union. Ukraine announced its independence the same year.

Russia's neighbors in Eastern Europe are concerned its invasion of Ukraine could trigger a wider conflict, and drones flying into its airspace have fueled jitters.

Moldova's Ministry of Defense said Thursday that five drones breached its airspace overnight, but it didn't specify who fired them.

Ukraine's air force said defenses shot down or suppressed seven Russian ballistic missiles, though it didn't say how they achieved that.

Four districts of Kyiv were hit during the night, damaging residential buildings, a school and a medical facility, though no casualties were reported, city police said.

Russian forces struck industrial facilities as well as energy infrastructure in Ukraine's central Poltava region, said Vitalii Diakivnych, head of the Poltava regional military administration.

The southern Odesa region also came under a major Russian attack lasting more than seven hours, according to Oleh Kiper, head of the Odesa regional military administration.

The barrage damaged a 16-story residential building and two educational facilities as well as a grain elevator, he said. Odesa is a key port for Ukraine's vital exports of grain and other agricultural products.

Some trains were delayed by more than 17 hours following the attack, according to Ukrainian state rail company Ukrzaliznysia.

Ukraine has also fired hundreds of long-range drones almost nightly at targets in Russia.

Ukraine's General Staff said that plane-launched missiles hit Russia's main and backup command posts near the eastern city of Donetsk, where Ukrainian defenders are under pressure from a Russian push.

The Russian Defense Ministry said Thursday that its air defenses shot down 267 Ukrainian drones over 14 Russian regions, the illegally annexed Crimean Peninsula, the Sea of Azov and the Black Sea.

After razing huge warehouses in recent months belonging to Wildberries, Russia's biggest online retailer, Ukrainian drones are now taking aim at Ozon, the country's second-largest e-commerce company.

Ozon initially said that its logistics facilities in the cities of Orenburg and Ufa were attacked, but neither of the premises caught fire. A later alteration to the company statement said that only the Ufa site was attacked, while the Orenburg facility was evacuated because of an alert, but resumed normal operations.

title: Ukraine file complaint over FIA lifting Russia ban
description: The Ukrainian Automobile Federation requests an urgent investigation into its Russian counterpart, the RAF.
fullText:
Ukraine has lodged a formal complaint with the ethics committee of motorsport's governing body the FIA following the decision to lift the ban on Russian competitors in international events.

The Ukrainian Automobile Federation (FAU) has requested an urgent investigation into its Russian counterpart, the RAF.

The ban on individuals from Russia and Belarus competing in international motorsport events had been in place since Russia launched its invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

The move was approved by the FIA world council, to which sources have told BBC Sport it was proposed by FIA president Mohammed ben Sulayem.

The FAU says the Russian Automobile Federation has "opened and continues to operate" offices in regions of Ukraine occupied by Russia - Crimea, the city of Sevastopol and the Donetsk and Zaporizhzhia Oblasts.

These are recognised by the United Nations as sovereign Ukrainian territory.

The FAU says these actions are in breach of both the FIA statutes and its international sporting code, which permit only one automobile club per country.

FAU president Oleksandr Feldman said: "This is a clear breach of the FIA statutes by the Russian Automobile Federation, which, as an FIA member organisation, is bound to comply with them.

"We urge the FIA president to take urgent action to have these offices closed, and for the Russian automobile federation to be sanctioned for its actions."

The Ukrainian club has requested the FIA ethics committee find the RAF in breach of FIA statutes and order it to close the offices with immediate effect.

The statement also points out that the head of the RAF, Boris Rotenberg, is "directly subject to international sanctions imposed by the US, UK, EU, and other allied jurisdictions in response to aggression against Ukraine".

The decision to lift the ban on Russian and Belarusian competitors followed a similar move by the International Olympic Association.

Following changes to the FIA statutes last year, the FIA ethics committee is under the control of Ben Sulayem and his ally the president of the senate, Carmelo Sanz de Barros.

The FIA has been approached for comment.

title: A Wildberries depot in Russia is destroyed as Ukraine extends its drone campaign
description: Long-range Ukrainian drones struck a major warehouse belonging to Russia’s biggest online retailer, burning it to the ground, local authorities said Wednesday.  The depot in the Tambov region southeas...
fullText:
Long-range Ukrainian drones struck a major warehouse belonging to Russia's biggest online retailer, burning it to the ground, local authorities said Wednesday.

The depot in the Tambov region southeast of Moscow had been hit on July 18, killing seven people. That attack was the start of Ukraine's aerial campaign that has delivered repeated blows to Russian e-commerce giant Wildberries. The company's size and commercial importance brought comparisons with Amazon.

Ukraine's cutting-edge drone capabilities developed since Russian President Vladimir Putin launched his full-scale invasion in 2022 have allowed Kyiv to hit Wildberries facilities across the country in recent weeks. Ukraine says goods sold by the company include equipment and technical components that are used by the Russian military, which the company denies. The attacks have unsettled Russians living far from the front and hurt small businesses.

Ukraine also has targeted oil facilities that are the backbone of the economy in Russia, which is one of the world's largest energy producers.

Ukraine's General Staff said its forces struck a Lukoil refinery overnight in Kstovo, in Russia's Nizhny Novgorod region. The facility, which has an annual processing capacity of about 125 million barrels, was set ablaze in the attack, a General Staff statement said.

Nizhny Novgorod has been targeted repeatedly by Ukraine. Gov. Gleb Nikitin confirmed the attack and said an unspecified "industrial facility" was damaged, without elaborating.

The relentless barrages prompted Russian President Vladimir Putin to decree that the state can temporarily seize control of critical infrastructure facilities if private owners don't protect them from Ukrainian drone attacks or don't rebuild them after the strikes. Analysts said the move aimed to compel companies to pay for their own security and bring damaged assets back into service, despite the cost.

Russia has hit Ukraine with ballistic and cruise missiles, powerful glide bombs and jet-powered drones, killing thousands of civilians. A woman and a 4-year-old were killed in a strike on a residential building in northern Ukraine's Chernihiv region, emergency services said Wednesday.

Ukraine has launched hundreds of drones at Russia almost nightly, hoping to overwhelm air defenses. The Russian Defense Ministry said that its forces overnight shot down 426 Ukrainian drones over 15 Russian regions as well as the Crimean Peninsula, which was illegally annexed by Moscow in 2014.

Ukraine struck Russian oil facilities, airfields, logistics and infrastructure, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in a social media post Wednesday. He didn't elaborate on the targets.

Also on Wednesday, Zelenskyy awarded Elon Musk Ukraine's Order of Freedom, one of its highest honors, for his "outstanding personal merits" in protecting human life and freedom and strengthening ties with the United States.

Musk is one of the most influential, and contentious, private sector figures in Ukraine's war effort. His satellite internet network Starlink has become deeply embedded in Ukraine's military operations, with commanders and soldiers relying on satellite connectivity to communicate and coordinate operations.

Starlink doesn't currently operate over Russian territory, but Zelenskyy wants Musk to reconsider and allow Ukrainian forces to maintain satellite connectivity for longer-range drone attacks targeting Russia's military and economic infrastructure.

The overnight attack on the Wildberries facility in Tambov was confirmed by the company, which said the depot was evacuated. It didn't say the extent of the damage.

Tambov Gov. Yevgeny Pervyshov said the fire destroyed the logistical center and injured two people.

Elsewhere, two people were killed and two others were wounded in Russia's Lipetsk region, south of Moscow, after a drone fell on a house, setting it ablaze, Gov. Igor Artamonov said.

title: Moscow airports disrupted amid Ukraine drone attacks following CIA director's visit

fullText:
Ukraine resumed drone attacks on Moscow overnight into Wednesday morning, the city's Mayor Sergey Sobyanin said, hours after the departure of the plane that carried CIA Director John Ratcliffe to Moscow for an unannounced visit on Tuesday morning.

Ukraine agreed to a U.S. request not to launch drone or missile strikes against Moscow during Ratcliffe's visit, a Ukrainian official told ABC News on Tuesday.

At least 10 drones were shot down while flying toward Moscow, Sobyanin said in a post to Telegram in the early hours of Wednesday morning. "Emergency services specialists are working at the crash site of the debris," the mayor said.

Russia's federal air transport agency, Rosaviatsiya, reported temporary flight restrictions at three of Moscow's four international airports -- Domodedovo, Zhukovsky and Vnukovo -- amid the overnight attacks. Ratcliffe's plane landed at Vnukovo on Tuesday morning and departed hours later, according to Flightradar24.

CIA Director John Ratcliffe in Moscow for meetings, sources say

Flight restrictions were also introduced at airports in Kaluga, Tambov, Penza, Saratov, Saransk, Cheboksary, Nizhny Novgorod, Kazan and Yaroslavl, Rosaviatsiya said in posts to Telegram.

The drones intercepted over Moscow were among the 426 Ukrainian craft claimed shot down overnight by the Russian Defense Ministry. Drones were intercepted over 15 Russian regions and occupied Crimea, the ministry said in a post to Telegram.

Among the targets hit was a Wildberries e-commerce facility in the city of Kotovsk in the Tambov region. Wildberries released a statement confirming the latest attack and said that all new shipments to the affected center had been suspended.

Local Gov. Yevgeny Pervyshov said in a post to Telegram that the strikes "caused a fire at the Wildberries logistics center. The fire covered an area of more than 100,000 square meters.

Elsewhere, Russian media reports indicated an attack on a major oil refinery in the Nizhny Novgorod region, in the city of Kstovoa.

Russia's escalating strikes in Ukraine increasingly spilling into NATO, Romania says

Regional Gov. Gleb Nikitin said in a post to Telegram that local defenses repelled an attack consisting of more than 40 drones.

"One industrial facility, several residential buildings, and cars sustained damage. Specialists are working at the site where debris fell, and efforts are underway to mitigate the consequences of the incident," Nikitin wrote.

The Ukrainian defense company Fire Point -- which produces drones and cruise missiles -- said in a post to Telegram that its munitions were used to attack both the Wildberries facility in Tambov and the oil refinery in Nizhny Novgorod.

Ukraine's General Staff also confirmed the attack on the refinery in Kstovoa, which it said is operated by the Lukoil corporation and "is involved in supplying the Russian Armed Forces."

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in a post to social media on Wednesday that Ukrainian forces "targeted 16 facilities in Russia" over the previous 24 hours, including oil facilities, airfields and a missile unit.

"The war must return to where it came from," he wrote. "Ukraine is responding to Russian attacks, and doing so in a way that ensures the cost of the war for the aggressor will inevitably increase. We are effectively reducing Russia's potential for aggression."

'The damage is enormous': Ukraine grapples with record-breaking Russian missile strikes

In Crimea, Sevastopol Gov. Mikhail Razvozhayev said that three incoming Ukrainian FP-5 Flamingo cruise missiles were shot down over the Black Sea.

Local officials reported that drone attacks elsewhere in Russia killed two people and injured nine others. Both of those killed died when a drone crashed into a home in the Lipetsk region, according to local officials. Injuries were reported in Lipetsk, Belgorod, Voronezh and Tula, local authorities said.

Ukraine's air force meanwhile, said Russia launched 162 drones into the country overnight and into Wednesday morning, of which 134 were intercepted or otherwise suppressed. The air force reported confirmed hits by enemy drones in 18 locations.

Ukraine's State Emergency Service said in posts to Telegram that a woman and a 4-year-old girl were killed in a Russian attack in the northern Chernihiv region, with a 14-year-old girl also injured.

The SES also reported Russian attacks and subsequent fires in the Sumy and Kherson regions, though said no casualties were reported in either location.

ABC News' Oleksiy Pshemyskiy and Tom Soufi Burridge contributed to this report.

title: Prominent Ukrainian commanders to lead defence of eastern region demanded by Russia

fullText:
KYIV, Aug 26 (Reuters) - President Volodymyr Zelenskiy has appointed two of Ukraine's most prominent commanders to oversee the defence of the country's eastern strongholds, as Kyiv struggles to beat back ‌a Russian onslaught on a region at the centre of stalled peace talks.

Moscow's troops are grinding towards the ‌so-called fortress belt of industrialised cities in the Donetsk region, which the Kremlin has demanded that Ukraine give up before it ends its war.

Visiting the front ​line with his new top general, Zelenskiy said Third Army Corps leader Andrii Biletskyi and Denys Prokopenko, commander of the First Corps Azov, will head new groupings aimed at strengthening defences around Donetsk.

Both men represent a new generation of experienced field commanders and currently lead what are seen as some of Kyiv's most capable and best-trained forces. Both their corps are already involved in defending that ‌part of the front, and the commanders ⁠have been praised for their combat efficiency and planning.

The announcement comes as Ukrainian troops face mixed success along the 1,200-km front line, where they began seizing back the initiative earlier ⁠this year.

They liberated several-dozen settlements this year during a several-stage operation in a southeastern sector, clawing back more than 700 sq. km. of territory, Zelenskiy said.

But Russian forces are also bearing down on the cities of Kostiantynivka, Kramatorsk and Sloviansk - all critical strongholds for Ukraine, ​which ​has dismissed Kremlin demands that it cede the region to end the ​more than four-year war.

Moscow's troops are infiltrating deeper ‌into Kostiantynivka, where the Ukrainians are being forced to weed them out from houses, basements and ruins, according to open-source mapping group Deep State.

Russia is also stepping up its air and artillery attacks on Kramatorsk and Sloviansk - where its forces are just 13 km away - to prepare for a targeted offensive on those cities, the group added.

Ukrainian military analyst Mykola Bielieskov said the appointment of Biletskyi and Prokopenko - both of whom have been at war since Russia's first invasion in 2014 - was intended ‌to give the new top commander Mykhailo Drapatyi greater scope for strategic ​planning.

His predecessor, Oleksandr Syrskyi, had been criticised for micromanaging even smaller sectors ​of the front.

"In other words, this is the right ​move," said Bielieskov.

Biletskyi, a prominent right-wing political leader, founded Ukraine's Azov Battalion in 2014 to fight Russian-backed ‌separatists. He later established the Third Army Corps ​as one of Ukraine's most sought-after ​units for new recruits.

Prokopenko commanded Azov through Moscow's siege of Mariupol and the Azovstal steel plant, and after his return from captivity in Russia, he helped build it into a force of tens of thousands.

Both units are known ​for embracing NATO-style doctrine and new technology.

Ukrainian ‌drone forces commander Robert Brovdi, a leader of Kyiv's mid- and long-range strike campaigns, praised the appointment as ​an important step towards "network-centric warfare".

"This is exactly what 'Smart War' is," he wrote on social media.

fullText:
London and Kyiv in deal to help stop protesters and hostile states targeting military bases and critical infrastructure

AI models trained on Ukrainian battlefield data will be used to stop protesters and foreign states targeting UK defence sites, railways and energy plants under a deal struck between London and Kyiv.

Private companies will also be given access to the vast trove of data from Ukraine’s Avengers AI lab to help build new systems, the first agreement of its kind in the UK.

The scheme will be piloted at a UK defence site, building a model to identify protesters or a hostile-state attack. It uses AI-optimised sensors in buried fibre-optic cables to detect different kinds of movement.

The government has suggested the technology, if proven workable, could be used at airports, prisons, railways and energy infrastructure.

The controversial proscription of the activist group Palestine Action was sparked after the group breached RAF Brize Norton on scooters last June, a highly embarrassing security lapse as a result of which the group was able to deface two military aircraft with spray paint before escaping the site without being detained.

Palestine Action said at the time that it had targeted RAF Voyager aircraft used for transport and refuelling, and that “activists have interrupted Britain’s direct participation in the commission of genocide and war crimes across the Middle East”.

Private companies will be able to access the data once approved by the MoD on a secure platform, though the data sharing is likely to raise alarm among privacy campaigners.

Pilot projects have already been approved with three British AI companies – Sintela, Mind Foundry and Skyral. Sintela, a Bristol-based company that specialises in fibre-optic sensors, recently struck a $35m (£26m) deal with the Trump administration to provide surveillance on the US-Mexico border.

The partnership with the Ukrainian AI lab means new UK security systems can be trained on operational drone datasets, strike mission footage and flight profiles, likely to include Russian sabotage attempts against critical Ukrainian infrastructure.

The cache of four years’ worth of military data contains a far deeper picture than models outside Ukraine have previously been trained on, which had been mostly restricted to open-source data.

The government eventually hopes to use the AI models to predict quickly when infrastructure such as railways, the power grid or military bases might be coming under threat or stress from hostile actors.

That would primarily come from the laying of fibre-optic cables that are able to identify unique movements of people or vehicles around sensitive sites. Ministry of Defence sources said that would specifically include when a site might be targeted by protesters – not just hostile states.

The prime minister, Andy Burnham, said it would be an opportunity for British companies to combine their AI expertise with Ukraine’s battlefield data, which would “accelerate the development of capabilities that not only strengthen our national security but better protect our critical infrastructure and growth in every postcode here at home”.

Other potential projects could include new AI chips to power drones, robotics and automated weapons systems.

Steven Murdoch, a professor of computer science at University College London, said technologies to detect movement from sensors in fibre-optic cables had been around for decades and that it was unclear if data from Ukraine would refine their capabilities.

“I haven’t heard anything that is very convincing, but there is a plausible scenario where they could see something that could be predicted easily and isn’t in any publicly known dataset,” he said.

Ukraine, however, has a lot of other data that may be valuable, especially related to new threats that countries in western Europe might face in the short to medium term.

“What’s valuable is something we’re seeing today which other countries will be worrying about in the future,” Murdoch said. “Anything to do with drones, for example.”

The defence secretary, Wes Streeting, said Ukraine was “pushing the frontier of defence innovation as they bravely resist Putin’s illegal invasion”.

“By combining the UK’s world-leading scientists, engineers and tech companies with Ukraine’s unique battlefield experience and data, we will strengthen both of our nations’ defence and security,” he said.

title: A women's shelter for refugees in Poland fights for survival as anti-Ukrainian sentiment rises
description: When Nastya Podorozhnya's relatives fled the war in Ukraine for neighboring Poland, volunteers welcomed them with open arms.  Podorozhnya, 29, was already living in Poland when the war began.  As she ...
fullText:
KRAKOW, Poland (AP) — When Nastya Podorozhnya's relatives fled the war in Ukraine for neighboring Poland, volunteers welcomed them with open arms.

Podorozhnya, 29, was already living in Poland when the war began. But days before Russia's full-scale invasion on Feb. 24, 2022, she rushed back to Ukraine to help her sister and nieces get out.

As she returned to Poland alongside an influx of refugees in the war's first days, she witnessed the outpouring of support from Polish volunteers. But she also spotted a risk: Ukrainian women accepting help from strangers could become vulnerable to human traffickers.

That was when she decided to found Martynka, a helpline and support group for female Ukrainian refugees escaping gender-based violence.

Four years later, she is struggling to keep the organization afloat. Funding for refugee support is drying up, hostility toward Ukrainians is growing, and Poland still lacks a long-term integration strategy. As war fatigue deepens, politicians are increasingly exploiting anti-refugee sentiment for political gain.

The shift is being felt by groups such as Martynka. While fundraising was relatively easy in the first months of the war, international donors have since turned their attention to other global crises.

Martynka's shelter, located in an inconspicuous two-bedroom apartment in central Krakow, has hosted more than 100 women and children. Women receive help to escape abusers and access medical care, psychological support, jobs and housing.

"It often starts with me having tea in this very kitchen with the women and they tell me what happened to them and I say 'girl, same,'" Podorozhnya told The Associated Press during an interview in the Krakow shelter, referring to her own experience of a man trying to rape her on a street in Poland in 2016.

As Podorozhnya and her colleagues struggle to raise enough money to keep the shelter open, she says calls for donations frequently trigger a torrent of online abuse.

"It's because I'm Ukrainian," she said.

Around 3.5 million Ukrainians fled to Poland in the first weeks of the war, according to the U.N. Poles greeted them at train stations and opened their homes to them, while the government granted refugees access to jobs and social security benefits.

The two countries share a long history of brutality at the hands of Russia, and Poland remains a key ally to Ukraine in the war.

In addition to the refugees, most of whom are women and children, more than 1 million Ukrainians were already living in Poland before the war, primarily as economic migrants.

The refugees have increasingly become targets of anti-Ukrainian rhetoric. In research published this year, Ukrainian migrants interviewed by Olena Babakova, a researcher at Warsaw's Vistula University, identified the 2025 Polish presidential campaign as the period when anti-Ukrainian feeling intensified, as it became a common theme for all parties, not just the far right.

Karol Nawrocki, representing the national-conservative camp and who eventually won the presidency, promised legislation that would prioritize Polish citizens over Ukrainians when accessing public services. Rafał Trzaskowski, the liberal candidate, proposed restricting child welfare benefits for Ukrainians.

As tensions increased, historical grievances between the countries resurfaced.

In June, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyydecided to name a military unit after a Ukrainian paramilitary organization accused of massacring Poles during World War II, causing outrage in Poland. Nawrocki responded by withdrawing a state honor awarded to Zelenskyy, further escalating the tensions.

"And it's not only negative feelings, Ukrainians really experience hostile conversations and attacks," Babakova told the AP.

According to data from the Polish police, 180 Ukrainian citizens were victims of prejudice-motivated crimes by mid-July, a significant increase compared with 275 for the whole of 2025 and 267 in 2024.

In response to multiple media reports of Ukrainians beaten on Polish streets over the summer, Prime Minister Donald Tusk said in late July that "we must wage war on violence and hatred."

The Polish government has been steadily cutting support for Ukrainian refugees, saying that many have stabilized their situation.

Poland's ombudsman has warned that the changes disproportionately affect the most vulnerable groups, including single mothers with several children, older people and those with chronic illnesses or disabilities. Because most Ukrainian men of military age, between 23 and 60, are prohibited from leaving the country, single mothers are overrepresented among the refugees.

Yuliia Repenko from the Ukrainian House said that her nongovernmental organization, which provides help to Ukrainians, was "increasingly supporting people who are particularly vulnerable to exclusion."

The Polish government has defended its decision to cut back aid to Ukrainian refugees. Katarzyna Nowakowska, Poland's deputy minister for family, labor and social policy, told the AP that the most vulnerable applicants still receive direct help from the state and any other refugees needing support should turn to social workers.

As the Polish government has been scaling back its support, international aid has also declined, further limiting options. Data from the U.N. refugee agency shows a steady drop since 2022 in the funding provided by international donors for Ukrainians, with only half the agency's identified needs financed this year, compared with 94% in 2022.

"Financial supporters have moved on from helping Ukrainian refugees, but the war is still ongoing," said Sonia Novytska, a Martynka helpline worker. "If anything, it has become deadlier since the start."

Martynka received about 1,800 requests for help last year, and staff expect that number to increase, Novytska said. Not only victims of violence contact the helpline now, but also mothers struggling to provide food and shelter for their children.

"What Poles need to understand is that we are helping the people that could otherwise become homeless in their neighborhoods, the people who might start abusing substances out of despair they can't make ends meet," Podorozhnya said.
